Bard

/BAHRD/ - rhymes with yard · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bard means a poet, often a singer as well.

Carved over the concert hall's door is a bard with his harp, mid-verse, mouth open in stone song.

Worked Example

When the mine closed, a retired welder became the town's bard: he set the shutdown, the picket winter, and the last cage-lift down in rhyming stanzas and sang them at the union hall until everyone under thirty knew the story by heart.

Bard fits because a bard is a poet, often a singer as well — he did not just report what happened; he made it memory, composed in verse and carried aloud. A narrator only tells a story; a bard composes it, keeps it, and sings a community's own life back to it.

How Bard Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

minstrel

minstrel: a working entertainer singing for supper, not for a people's memory

troubadour

troubadour: a courtly singer, love songs above all

Antonyms

scribe

scribe: writes down what others say and sings nothing

mime

mime: performs without a single word

How Strong Is It? — rhymer → storyteller → bard

rhymer vs. bard

rhymer vs. bard: A rhymer is the hobbyist rung — birthday couplets and refrigerator verse, nothing meant to outlive the party.

storyteller vs. bard

storyteller vs. bard: A storyteller stops short of a bard — the tales may hold a room, but a bard shapes them into verse and song and carries a whole people's memory in them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bard

Root — bard: poet-singer (Celtic bardos, borrowed whole)

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: bard came into English whole from Celtic — Welsh bardd, Gaelic bàrd — where it named the tribe's honored poet-singer. For centuries English used it as an insult for wandering versifiers, until admiration for Shakespeare, 'the Bard,' polished it back to glory.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Celtic bardos left no other everyday English word behind — bard is the root, whole and alone. When England crowned Shakespeare 'the Bard of Avon,' the old Celtic title had become the highest compliment poetry offers.

Word Building

Word Choice

literary / historical

Bard carries honor and age: use it for poets who sing a community's memory, or, capital-B, for Shakespeare. This unit's narrator tells a story aloud without composing it; a minstrel entertains for pay. Calling a modern songwriter a bard is pointed praise, not plain description.
